strengths: Clear problem motivation: articulates three unavoidable sources of off-policy mismatch in LLM-RL (implementation divergence, MoE routing, distributed staleness) with concrete technical details

Tighter theoretical bounds: derives meaningful improvements over O(T²) TRPO bounds with Pinsker-Marginal O(T^{3/2}) and Mixed O(T) variants, with concrete numerical examples showing 48-200× improvement
Key theoretical insight: rigorously identifies that D^{tok,max}_{KL} is a sequence-level quantity that token-level methods cannot control, supported by formal proof (Proposition C.1)
Sound mathematical analysis: proofs of Theorems 3.1-3.2 correctly apply Pinsker's inequality to tightened bounds; key lemmas (B.1-B.4) are properly established
Comprehensive failure analysis: Section 4 provides detailed mechanistic explanations for why PPO clipping (gradient leakage table) and token masking fail to control sequence-level divergence
Thorough treatment of approximations: Appendix D carefully analyzes sample-based divergence estimators (k₃, |log ρ|) and their properties and limitations
weaknesses: Critical gap—complete absence of empirical validation: no experiments on any LLM-RL task, no measurement of masking rates or sample efficiency, no evidence that theoretical bounds are meaningful or that TRM actually improves training in practice

Severely limited algorithmic novelty: TRM is a straightforward application of the bounds without algorithmic innovation; the core contribution is theoretical tightening of known bounds using standard techniques (Pinsker's inequality)

Inadequate practical analysis of sample efficiency: paper acknowledges max criterion 'may mask many sequences under high MoE noise' but provides no quantitative analysis, convergence rates, or solutions; unclear how aggressive masking affects learning dynamics and sample complexity

Gap between theory and practice: rigorous guarantees require exact KL computation (Theorem 5.1), but Section D admits sample-based approximations provide no formal bounds; 'average criterion' relaxation explicitly trades theoretical tightness without analyzing impact

No principled hyperparameter guidance: threshold δ selection lacks any practical guidance; no sensitivity analysis provided; no discussion of warm-start or curriculum strategies when divergence is initially large
Missing convergence analysis: only establishes single-step monotonic improvement, not convergence rates; no sample complexity analysis for the effective batch size reduction from masking
Incomplete treatment of assumptions: R ∈ [0, 1] bound is restrictive; handling of variable-length sequences unclear; no explicit statement of required context visitation probability assumptions
Reproducibility concerns: no code, no specification of exact KL computation in practice, no dataset/task details, algorithm details sparse (gradient normalization by N vs accepted count ambiguous)

Limited engagement with related work: Liu et al. (2025) and Yao et al. (2025) cited for off-policy mismatch but not substantively engaged; no comparison with other off-policy divergence management approaches in LLM-RL

Presentation gaps: Section 4's argument that token masking doesn't reduce D^{tok,max}_{KL} is somewhat obvious in retrospect; Algorithm 1 is trivial; the minorizer M(πθ) concept appears briefly without formal development

strengths: Solid theoretical contribution: Derives tighter O(T^{3/2}) and O(T) bounds versus classical O(T²), achieving 48-200× improvements on concrete examples

Key insight well-articulated: Clearly identifies that D^{tok,max}_KL is inherently sequence-level and unreachable by token-independent methods like PPO clipping, with compelling 'fundamental dilemma' argument
Mathematically sound analysis: Proofs appear correct; clever application of Pinsker's inequality to marginal KL divergences is novel and technically rigorous
Clear problem motivation: Concretely demonstrates that classical bounds become vacuous for long sequences (T=4096 gives error ≈1677 with D^{tok,max}_KL = 10^{-4})
Well-structured presentation: Clearly written with helpful concrete examples, systematic treatment of background, and detailed appendix with proofs
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Complete absence of any empirical validation—zero experiments. No evidence that bounds are non-vacuous in practice, no performance comparisons with baselines, no analysis of masking rates, no computational cost measurement. This alone is sufficient grounds for rejection from ICML

Unknown practical applicability: We don't know if D^{tok,max}_KL is actually small in real LLM-RL systems, what fraction of sequences TRM masks in practice (paper acknowledges it 'may mask many sequences' but provides no data), or whether sample efficiency penalty outweighs theoretical gains

Sample-based approximations undermine theory: Practical versions (k₃ estimator, |log ρ|) are acknowledged as 'approximate detectors' without rigorous guarantees; if practitioners use these, theoretical guarantees no longer hold
Unclear parameter selection: No guidance on how to choose δ threshold in practice or how it should adapt during training
Computational overhead not addressed: Storing full rollout logits and computing exact KL for every token at every position carries real cost; feasibility for large-scale LLM-RL unknown
Limited algorithmic novelty: Once accepting the theoretical argument, the solution (exclude violating sequences) is straightforward; the algorithm itself is a simple threshold
Overstated claims: Off-policy mismatch claimed 'unavoidable' but relies on very recent preprints; no empirical measurement of D^{tok,max}_KL in real systems shows it's actually problematic
Missing ablations: No analysis of soft masking as alternative, no exploration of integration with KL-penalty-based rewards, no threshold sensitivity analysis
Technical gaps: Pinsker bound may be loose for multimodal distributions; sample-based approximations have single sample per context so guarantees remain approximate

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling motivation: off-policy mismatch in modern LLM-RL is real and practically important
Strong theoretical contributions: Pinsker-Marginal bound at O(T^3/2) and Mixed bound at O(T) are substantially tighter (48-200×) than classical O(T^2) TRPO bound
Elegant insight about sequence-level control: clear demonstration that D^tok,max_KL is inherent to sequences and cannot be controlled by token-level methods like PPO clipping or token masking
Clean algorithmic solution: TRM is simple, implementable, and directly addresses the theoretical limitation with a clear masking criterion
Rigorous mathematical exposition: all proofs are sound, key lemmas are well-established, and the logic is clear throughout
Good presentation quality: well-organized paper with clear motivation, clean notation, and honest limitations discussion
Length-invariant trust region threshold: δ does not need to grow with sequence length T, which is a practical advantage
weaknesses: Critical: Complete absence of empirical validation - no experiments on any tasks (synthetic, small-scale, or realistic). No evidence that TRM improves practical performance, no measurement of masking rates, no comparison to PPO or baselines
Unclear practical applicability: no principled method for setting δ in practice; choice of δ = 10^-4 for T=4096 appears arbitrary
Masking efficiency problem: paper acknowledges that max criterion 'may mask many sequences under high MoE noise' but provides no quantification or analysis of implications for sample efficiency

Disconnect between theory and practice: rigorous guarantee requires exact KL computation with stored logits, but Appendix D's sample-based approximations are acknowledged as non-rigorous 'approximate detectors' without bounds
Average-criterion relaxation lacks justification: proposed (1/T)∑D_KL ≤ δ_avg does not guarantee D^tok,max_KL ≤ δ, so monotonic improvement guarantee is lost
Restrictive assumptions: bounded rewards R ∈ [0,1] is limiting; extension to unbounded rewards is deferred to future work
Incomplete convergence analysis: no sample complexity bounds, convergence rates, or analysis of what happens when πroll and πθ diverge faster than masking can control
Limited technical novelty in derivations: while the bounds are tighter, techniques (Pinsker + chain rule) are standard; clever application but not methodologically groundbreaking

Weak empirical foundation for off-policy mismatch claim: relies on unpublished concurrent work (Liu et al. 2025, Yao et al. 2025) for evidence that mismatch is unavoidable; magnitude in realistic settings unclear
Theorem 5.1 monotonic improvement guarantee: may be vacuous when many sequences are masked and L_masked → 0; no analysis of when guarantee is non-trivial

strengths: Identifies a fundamental theoretical limitation of classical trust region bounds for long-horizon LLM-RL and provides a concrete, compelling example (T=4096 yields error bound ≈1677, vacuous for unit rewards)
Novel theoretical contributions: Pinsker-Marginal bound (O(T^3/2)), Mixed bound (O(T)), and Adaptive bound via importance-ratio decomposition that strictly generalizes the Pinsker-Marginal bound
Rigorous mathematical analysis with correct proofs throughout; the importance-ratio decomposition with adaptive per-position Pinsker application is creative and technically sound
Proposition 4.8 provides an elegant impossibility result showing D_tok,max_KL cannot be bounded by D_seq_KL, rigorously justifying sequence-level (not token-level) constraints

Clear analysis of why token-level methods fail (Section 5): PPO clipping suffers gradient leakage on negative advantages with high importance ratios; token masking leaves D_tok,max_KL unchanged, keeping bounds vacuous
Practical algorithm (TRM) is simple, theoretically grounded, and comes with monotonic improvement guarantees when D_tok,max_KL ≤ δ holds globally
Comprehensive treatment with extensive appendices covering sample-based estimators, length-neutral variants (LN-TRM, SER), and detailed proofs demonstrating thoroughness
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 6.1 requires D_tok,max_KL ≤ δ to hold globally, but only verifies this empirically via batch acceptance rates (recommending ≥70% as 'reasonable confidence'). This undermines claims of 'first non-vacuous guarantees' if the global condition cannot be rigorously verified

Limited experimental validation: single task (AIME25), single model (Qwen3-8B), modest absolute improvements (0.15→0.25 score), no comparison to alternative stabilization methods or recent work (Liu et al. 2025, Yao et al. 2025), and missing ablation studies on threshold δ sensitivity

Fundamental sample efficiency concern unaddressed: TRM uses rejection sampling with 30-50% masking rates in experiments. No analysis of additional samples needed to compensate, nor comparison to methods reducing divergence at source (backend alignment, soft masking, importance weighting)

Length bias in basic TRM: acceptance probability decays as (1-p)^T, causing exponential rejection of long sequences (e.g., <2% acceptance at T=4096, p=10^-3). While LN-TRM is proposed in Appendix D, it is untested experimentally and not discussed as a primary contribution

Incomplete characterization of off-policy mismatch: three sources identified (backend, MoE, staleness) but relative magnitudes not quantified. Experiments artificially inject backend discrepancies; unclear if they reflect real deployment scenarios

Adaptive bound practicality unclear: computing per-position divergences D̄_t requires expectations over the rollout distribution. Implementation details and sample variance concerns not addressed. Data-dependent advantage of the bound not empirically validated

Sample-based estimators (k_2, k_3) are heuristics lacking rigorous justification. Paper admits full guarantees require exact KL; when logits cannot be stored, guarantees degrade to unvalidated approximations

Convergence and optimization quality not analyzed: paper bounds approximation error but doesn't analyze convergence rates or prove that larger L(πθ) translates to faster convergence. Figures lack error bars and statistical significance testing across multiple seeds

strengths: Solid theoretical contributions with three tighter error bounds (O(T³/²), O(T), and data-dependent adaptive bound) that significantly improve upon classical TRPO's O(T²) scaling
Novel Adaptive Bound (Theorem 4.6) cleverly combines importance-ratio decomposition with adaptive Pinsker application, with rigorous proofs

Clear and rigorous analysis of why token-level methods fail: Proposition 4.8 establishes that D_tok,max_KL cannot be bounded by sequence-level metrics, and Section 5 provides intuitive explanations of PPO clipping failure modes
Well-motivated problem with concrete illustration (T=4096, δ=10⁻⁴ yields 48× bound improvement)
Comprehensive treatment including multiple variants (TRM-Max, LN-TRM, SER) and detailed mathematical exposition with complete proofs
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only one task (AIME25), one model (Qwen3-8B), one training setup (Zero-RL with GRPO); no experiments on code generation, other reasoning tasks, or other model scales

Critical practical concerns unaddressed: actual sequence acceptance rates not reported; unclear if 30-50% rejection is computationally prohibitive; no sample efficiency analysis; no memory/computational cost discussion for storing rollout logits

No comparison to recent related work: Liu et al. (2025) and Yao et al. (2025) address similar off-policy mismatch issues but are cited without comparison; missing baselines beyond standard PPO clipping

Gap between theory and practice: Theorem 6.1 requires D_tok,max_KL ≤ δ globally but only empirically verifies via 70% acceptance rate (heuristic); LN-TRM in Appendix D weakens guarantees; length bias acknowledged but not resolved despite critical for long reasoning

Insufficient experimental rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds; no ablation studies on δ sensitivity; backend divergence simulation may not reflect real-world mismatch; uncontrolled hyperparameter choices (e.g., why lr=1e-6?)

Limited novelty in methodology: theoretical techniques (Pinsker's inequality, importance weighting, chain rules) are standard; sequence-level masking is relatively straightforward once the theory establishes max-token divergence is the bottleneck

Reproducibility concerns: many design choices lack justification; requires proprietary DAPO-MATH-17k dataset; no code release; critical sample-based estimators (k₂, k₃) relegated to appendix with only intuitive justification, not formal guarantees

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a critical practical problem: off-policy mismatch in long-horizon LLM-RL with vacuous O(T²) classical bounds, providing concrete numerical evidence (1677 vs. 8.2-35.0 for T=4096).

Novel theoretical insight that approximation error depends on D_tok,max_KL (sequence-level maximum), not average KL, with Proposition 4.8 formally proving this cannot be bounded by sequence-level divergence.
Three progressively tighter bounds: Pinsker-Marginal (O(T³/²)), Mixed (O(T)), and Adaptive (strictly tightens both via importance-ratio decomposition and adaptive per-position Pinsker application).
Rigorous analysis of why token-level methods fail: clear exposition of PPO clipping's asymmetric failure mode (Section 5, Table 2) showing unclipped gradients persist despite clipping.
Principled solution (TRM) directly enforcing theoretical preconditions with formal guarantees (Theorem 6.1), supported by clean rejection-sampling interpretation.

Comprehensive treatment including sample-based KL estimators with unbiasedness proofs, length-neutral variants (LN-TRM, SER), full proofs of complex results (importance-ratio decomposition), and detailed off-policy mismatch source analysis.
Empirical demonstration that standard PPO clipping causes training collapse while TRM maintains stability, with clear visualization of PPL Gap metric and AIME25 performance recovery.
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: single task (AIME25 on Qwen3-8B), only ~800 training steps, no comparison with alternative sequence-level masking or recent stabilization approaches, and no ablation studies (e.g., which of three bounds matters in practice?).

Critical gap between theory and practice: Theorem 6.1 requires global D_tok,max_KL ≤ δ, but TRM only verifies batch-wise conditions; Remark 6.2's 70% acceptance heuristic lacks rigor and has no analysis of violation consequences.

Sample efficiency not analyzed: rejecting entire sequences discards potentially useful data; early training divergence may be unavoidable; no comparison with unmasked methods or analysis of efficiency-stability trade-off.

Length bias systematically rejects long sequences with exponential decay (1−p)^T; for p=10⁻³, T=4096: ~98.3% rejection; this directly harms reasoning tasks (motivating application) requiring longer chains of thought; LN-TRM/SER mitigate but add complexity.

Practical hyperparameter selection is ad-hoc: Figure 3 shows single criteria insufficient (TRM-Max&Avg required), paper recommends monitoring PPL Gap (Section 7) rather than principled guidance; unclear how to choose δ systematically.

Missing key experimental comparisons: no head-to-head with alternative methods, no per-length acceptance rate analysis, no evaluation on sequences >4096 tokens (despite being motivating application), no ablation on which bound dominates in practice.

Theory-practice gaps on efficiency: per-position divergences D̄_t computation not detailed; sample-based estimators (k2, k3) lose theoretical guarantees but tightness loss unquantified; bounded reward assumption (R∈[0,1]) may not hold with unbounded advantage estimates (GRPO).

Incomplete guidance on variant selection: TRM-Max fails alone (Figure 3); paper offers LN-TRM and SER but doesn't systematically compare or recommend; practitioners must choose without clear criteria.

strengths: Novel theoretical contributions: derives a family of tighter bounds (O(T^3/2), O(T), data-dependent Adaptive) that significantly improve over classical O(T^2) bounds, with concrete 409× improvement for T=4096
Fundamental insight: Proposition 3.10 rigorously proves that maximum token-level divergence cannot be controlled from sequence-level quantities, motivating sequence-level masking
Multiple perspectives: KL-based and TV-based bounds with complementary strengths; Adaptive bound with per-position data-dependence elegantly dominates worst-case variants

Clear problem motivation: well-articulated sources of off-policy mismatch (backend discrepancies, MoE routing, staleness) with concrete numerical examples demonstrating vacuousness of classical bounds
Rigorous mathematical treatment: proofs are sound, error decomposition via importance-ratio tower property (Appendix D) is elegant, honest discussion of preconditions (Remark 4.3)
Practical awareness: acknowledges length bias, proposes sample-based approximations (k2, k3), and develops length-neutral variants (LN-TRM, SER)
Unified framework: Theorem 3.8 elegantly combines all bounds via minimum, providing tightest guarantee across divergence regimes
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: single benchmark (AIME25), single model size (8B), single algorithm (GRPO); no comparison to other masking strategies, alternative trust region methods, or baseline PPO configurations

Critical gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.2's precondition D^{tok,max}_{KL} ≤ δ cannot be guaranteed by the algorithm; TRM only filters for this condition, making the empirical acceptance rate a diagnostic rather than a guarantee

No evidence of performance improvement: Figures 1-3 demonstrate training stabilization (lower PPL gap) but provide minimal evidence of actual task performance gains; AIME25 scores across methods are similar (~0.25)

Missing ablations and analysis: no systematic ablation of threshold δ, masking criterion, or acceptance rates; no error bars or significance testing; parameter choices appear hand-tuned to single benchmark

Incomplete practical analysis: computational overhead of storing logits and computing full-vocabulary KL not quantified; sample efficiency loss from sequence rejection not evaluated; no guidance on threshold selection
Limited scalability evidence: only tested at small scale (8B model, batch size 32); generalization to larger models and domains unclear; length bias in main algorithm only addressed in appendices
Circular precondition issue: Algorithm 1 cannot establish that the global precondition holds; if empirical acceptance rate is low, the bound B* is invalid, leaving unclear what value TRM provides
No comparison to related work: missing direct experimental comparison to Liu et al. (2025), Yao et al. (2025), IMPALA-style corrections, or simple PPO variants with looser clipping

strengths: Sound theoretical analysis with rigorous derivations of multiple bound families combining KL and TV routes, including a novel adaptive bound with data-dependent per-position divergences
Clean negative result (Proposition 3.10) establishing that controlling average KL divergence is insufficient—must control the maximum
Well-motivated problem with concrete demonstration that classical O(T²) bounds become vacuous for realistic long-horizon settings (example: T=4096 gives bound ≈1677)
Comprehensive technical treatment with clear exposition of why token-level methods cannot control sequence-level quantities
Elegant hybrid bound that selects between KL and TV routes per position, strictly dominating either route alone
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.2 requires an unverifiable global precondition (D_tok,max_KL ≤ δ for all reachable contexts) that is likely violated when divergence is high. When this fails, the bound is invalid anyway, making claims about 'non-vacuous guarantees' misleading

Severely limited experimental validation: Only one experimental setup (Qwen3-8B on AIME25), no ablations, no baselines, no validation that bounds are non-vacuous in practice, and no analysis of acceptance rates or their correlation with performance

Unclear practical contribution: TRM is rejection sampling (not novel), and Remark 4.3 shows masking is 'redundant on-support' when the precondition holds—undermining the connection between theory and method

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuine practical problem (off-policy mismatch in LLM-RL) that is largely ignored by theory

Strong theoretical contributions: derives multiple complementary bound families (Pinsker-Marginal O(T^3/2), Mixed O(T), Adaptive) that achieve 409× improvement over classical O(T^2) bounds; unified bound elegantly combines KL and TV routes

Novel Adaptive bound (Theorem 3.6) uses per-position divergence D̄_t to strictly dominate worst-case bounds when divergence is non-uniform; shows Pinsker-Marginal and Coupling bounds are special cases
Key structural insight (Proposition 3.10) formally proves sequence-level divergence D^tok,max_KL cannot be controlled by functions of aggregate D^seq_KL, explaining why token-level methods fail
Section 4.1 provides concrete analysis of why PPO clipping and token masking are insufficient, distinguishing gradient leakage from policy-level guarantees

Rigorous mathematical development with multiple error decompositions (Performance Difference Identity and importance-ratio based), comprehensive proofs, and correct handling of different divergence regimes
Honest treatment of limitations and preconditions: Remark 4.3 provides sharp dichotomy between regimes where masking is redundant vs. moot; precondition-free guarantee provided despite costs
Simple, implementable algorithm (Algorithm 1) that reuses stored logits for exact KL; sample-based approximations for logits-unavailable case
Multiple algorithmic variants discussed (TRM-Max, TRM-Avg, LN-TRM, SER) showing awareness of practical considerations like length bias
